1.pericope_label: Woe to the land shadowing with wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia... That sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters

schools.summary: Delitzsch says flatly that the land is Ethiopia, against the expositors who make the strangely described people Israel, and holds that the oracle predicts the destruction of Sennacherib's army; the expedition was still impending, and the envoys are not sent to Judah for help but carry urgent commands to their own people. Ellicott names Tirhakah, whose movements from the upper Nile, subduing Egypt and preparing to meet the Assyrian, had raised the hopes of Hezekiah's counsellors who trusted in an arm of flesh; he takes the phrase about the river for the region of the White and Blue Nile, prefers among the readings of the wings the winged disk that marks Ethiopian sovereignty in Egyptian painting, confirming it from an inscription in which chiefs beg to be under an Ethiopian conqueror's shadow, and would drop the supplied word of saying so that the following clause becomes the prophet's own charge to the messengers, rendering the disputed pair tall and polished rather than scattered and peeled.

Gill lists the candidates for the land without choosing between them, Assyria, Judea, and Egypt or Ethiopia, rejects the notion that birds flocking to a hot country are meant by the wings, and proposes instead the mountains that encompass part of Ethiopia or the sails of ships; taking the word for ambassadors in its other sense of images, he passes on the conjecture that the vessels carried the head of one Egyptian god and the image of another. Calvin cannot determine the nation either, but rules out Egypt as a whole, since the next chapter treats Egypt separately, and rules out the Troglodytes, who by the old geographers had no intercourse with other nations and screeched like bats rather than spoke; on the boats he supplies the reason for their material, that the Nile is dangerous at the cataracts and wooden ships would be dashed on the rocks.

Clarke calls this one of the most obscure prophecies in the book, its subject, design, audience, occasion and both parties to the embassy all doubtful, though he supposes Egypt; he takes the shadowing wings for a musical instrument altogether, the winged cymbal, since the Hebrews had no name for the Egyptian sistrum, notes that vessels of papyrus suit Egypt exactly with two Latin authors for weaving ships from the plant, renders the first disputed term stretched out in length, Egypt being one long vale with the river down its middle, and takes the swift messengers for no particular persons but the ordinary carriers of news. Wesley leaves the land at Ethiopia beyond Egypt or Egypt, collects the scriptural uses of the word for battlements, an army and a ship's sails, adds that reed boats were cheaper, swifter and light enough to carry overland, and reads scattered of a people dwelling apart rather than banished, and peeled of hair plucked off as a figure of calamity.

Henry, weighing Egypt against an Ethiopia he places east of Canaan rather than in Africa, has Tirhakah offering the Jews the shadow of his wings by a diversion against Assyria, and God slighting the offer and taking his own course to protect Jerusalem.

debates.question: What land is shadowing with wings?

positions.view: Undetermined: Assyria, Judea, and Egypt or Ethiopia have all been proposed, the last most generally received.
Ethiopia, definitely; the people so described are not Israel.
Ethiopia under Tirhakah, newly master of Egypt and courting Hezekiah's party.
Probably Egypt, though subject, design, audience and occasion are all obscure.
Undeterminable, but not Egypt as a whole and not the Troglodytes.
Some neighbour of Israel, whether Egypt or an Ethiopia east of Canaan, whose offer of shelter God slights.
The mountains that shade part of Ethiopia, or the sails of ships.
Armies or ships, the word being used in Scripture of battlements, an army and a sail.
The winged disk of Egyptian painting, the emblem of Ethiopian sovereignty.
Not wings at all but a musical instrument, the winged cymbal or Egyptian sistrum.

outliers.note: Abandons the image entirely, reading the shadowing wings as the name of an Egyptian instrument the Hebrews had no word for because they did not use one.
Disposes of the Troglodytes as candidates by quoting the old geographers that they screeched like bats rather than speaking and had no dealings with other nations.

themes: Woe to the land shadowing with wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia:

That sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters, saying, Go, ye swift messengers, to a nation scattered and peeled, to a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation meted out and trodden down, whose land the rivers have spoiled!

3.pericope_label: All ye inhabitants of the world, and dwellers on the earth, see ye, when he lifteth up an ensign on the mountains... For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower

schools.summary: Ellicott leaves the agent of the signal out, rendering both clauses indefinitely, when an ensign is set up and a trumpet sounded, and hears the prophet calling every nation, Ethiopia included, to watch for a signal as distinct as a beacon-fire on a hill, proclaiming the downfall of Assyria. Delitzsch prints these verses with the next two and picks his comment up only at the last of them, asking what effect the act of God described here would have on the Ethiopian kingdom if it should now take place.

Gill offers two readings of the summons, that the prophet calls the world to be eye and ear witnesses of a judgment so manifest that all shall see it, or that the messengers address the doomed nation, assuring them that however secure they are they will soon see the sign and hear the alarm; on the vine he has the schemers' designs cut short before they are ripe for execution, though they had promised themselves a large harvest of their neighbours. Calvin argues that the verbs are future rather than imperative, since the most distant nations will be witnesses that the war originated not with men but with God, and observes that when wars are waged everyone sees plainly what is done but most men ascribe their beginning and end to chance; he prefers to read the connecting particle of the fourth verse as for rather than and, the prophet answering a doubt that would otherwise perplex weak minds, since when confusion arises a veil conceals the providence of God; and he finds his standing lesson in the vintage figure, that the wicked flourish and are spared until at the very moment the fruit is expected they are stripped of it and rooted out.

Clarke makes God the agent and takes the standard and trumpet for the meteors themselves, the thunder, lightning, storm and tempest accompanying the Assyrian army's destruction, comparing the Greek poet who has the wide earth crash and the great heaven sound like a trumpet as the gods go to battle; he states the argument of the rest of the chapter, that God would comfort his own people though they were threatened with immediate destruction and the Assyrian's expectations would be rendered abortive just as he thought them ripe; and he corrects the fifth verse, where a defective pointing has led many interpreters, our translators among them, to take the word for the vine's blossom as the predicate when it is the subject, since a swelling grape cannot become a blossom. Wesley has God gathering the nations by ensign and trumpet to execute his judgments, explains that God is said in Scripture to rest when he does not act on a people's behalf, reads the clear heat and the dew-cloud as influences that scorch and come unwelcome in harvest, and times the stroke at the moment the bud has turned into a grape and gives hope of a good vintage.

debates.question: Who lifts the ensign, and what is it?

positions.view: God, and the ensign and trumpet are the storm itself, the thunder and tempest that destroyed the Assyrian army.
Nobody named: both clauses are indefinite, a signal for the nations to watch for.
God, gathering the nations as by ensign and trumpet to execute judgment.
Either the prophet summoning the world as witnesses, or the messengers warning the doomed nation.
The verbs are future, not imperative: the distant nations will be witnesses that the war came from God.

debates.question: What does the cutting of the unripe vine signify?

positions.view: The frustration of the Assyrian's designs at the very moment he thought them ripe.
The schemers' plans cut short before execution, though they had promised themselves a large harvest.
The general rule that the wicked are spared to flourish and then stripped and rooted out with their offspring.
That instead of gathering the grapes he cuts down the tree.

outliers.note: Corrects the Authorised Version's grammar at the fifth verse on the ground that a swelling grape cannot become a blossom, the mispointed word being the subject and not the predicate.
Observes that although everyone sees plainly what happens in a war, most men ascribe its beginning and end to chance.

themes: All ye inhabitants of the world, and dwellers on the earth, see ye, when he lifteth up an ensign on the mountains; and when he bloweth a trumpet, hear ye.
For so the Lord said unto me, I will take my rest, and I will consider in my dwelling place like a clear heat upon herbs, and like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.
For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away and cut down the branches.

6.pericope_label: They shall be left together unto the fowls of the mountains, and to the beasts of the earth... In that time shall the present be brought unto the LORD of hosts of a people scattered and peeled

schools.summary: Ellicott says figure and reality are strangely blended, the grapes cut off being the carcases of the Assyrian host left unburied for the vultures; on the closing verse he takes the people to be themselves the gift, reading a people rather than of the people, and has the nation the prophet keeps describing instead of naming offer itself to God's service, finding the parallel in the psalm where Ethiopia stretches out her hands to God, and thinking the messengers who justified the prophet's words were perhaps among the envoys who later carried gifts to Jerusalem.

Gill allows the reading of the carcases and also the destruction of Ethiopians or Egyptians whose princes and people would fall together unburied, and dates the present not to the time of the destruction but to some time after, in gospel times. Calvin generalises the picture, the fallen being cast aside as worthless like the chaff on the dunghill in the Baptist's preaching, and men who thought themselves safe thrown down beneath all men and the beasts; on the closing verse he applies the words to the Jews, pointing back to the second verse where the same descriptions were used of them, and takes from a people to mean it will not be an entire nation but a feeble remnant that is offered in sacrifice. He draws from this the lesson for his own day, that however far the body of the Church is torn into fragments God will unite the members by his Spirit; he explains that the prophets describe worship by outward acts because worship is within the soul and can be set out only by signs; and he concludes that there is no other way of belonging to the Church than by being offered to God in sacrifice, and that it is not necessary to run to Jerusalem, since Zion is now as wide as the world.

Clarke keeps givers and gift apart, noting that the Egyptians were in alliance with Judah and fellow-sufferers under the same invader and so nearly interested in its deliverance, and that when many afterwards brought gifts to Jerusalem and presents to Hezekiah he does not doubt the Egyptians distinguished themselves; he then makes the textual point that decides how much the verse can carry, that the Greek and Latin read from a people rather than a people, confirmed by the repetition in the next line, so that on that reading the prediction of Egypt's admission into the true Church is not so explicit here as it might seem. Wesley keeps to the branches cut down and left with the unripe grapes on them, so that birds and beasts may shelter or feed there all year, and puts the present at or after the time when the judgment has been fully executed, with the people spoken of presenting themselves and their sacrifices to the true God.

debates.question: Who is the present brought to the Lord of hosts?

positions.view: The Ethiopians, who are themselves the gift, offering themselves to God's service.
The Egyptians, bringing gifts after the deliverance; and on the better reading the verse is not an explicit prediction of their admission to the Church.
The Jews, and only a remnant of them, the same people described in the second verse.
A people presenting themselves and their sacrifices to the true God, some time after the judgment, in gospel times.

debates.question: What are the fowls and beasts left to feed on?

positions.view: The unburied carcases of the Assyrian host, figure and reality being blended.
Either that, or the fallen princes and people of Ethiopia or Egypt lying unburied.
The wicked generally, disdained even by beasts, as chaff cast on the dunghill.
Literal cut branches with unripe grapes still on them, sheltering or feeding birds and beasts all year.

outliers.note: Turns the closing verse into an argument that Zion is now as wide as the world, so that belonging to the Church means being offered to God in sacrifice rather than going up to Jerusalem.

themes: They shall be left together unto the fowls of the mountains, and to the beasts of the earth: and the fowls shall summer upon them, and all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon them.

In that time shall the present be brought unto the Lord of hosts of a people scattered and peeled, and from a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation meted out and trodden under foot, whose land the rivers have spoiled, to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, the mount Zion.
